issues.description: The script file's value is being shipped through the RPC payload as a side-channel to a path that already exists.
issues.detail: COMPLECTED. The response now carries both an identity (pipeline_package_path) and the full value of a different artifact (script_content). Two facts about the world — 'where the compiled script lives' and 'what the script said at compile time' — are braided into one envelope. A separate read endpoint keyed by path keeps the value request explicit and lets the client ask for it only when the user clicks download.

issues.description: compiledContent duplicates compiledPath as a place-oriented snapshot with no time semantics.
issues.detail: PLACE-ORIENTED. The state now holds the path (an identity pointing at a file on disk) and a string copy of that file's contents at one moment. Nothing says when the copy was taken or whether the file has since changed. If a later compile mutates the file but the panel still holds the prior string, the download will silently disagree with the path. Make the time explicit or fetch on click.

issues.description: Reading the script unconditionally complects compilation with serving a download.
issues.detail: Compilation's job is to produce artifacts on disk and return where they are. Reading the file back into memory and returning it inline mixes 'I compiled' with 'I am also a file server.' Every caller now pays the read and the payload size whether or not anyone will click download. Separate the two operations; let the click drive the read.

issues.description: handleDownloadClick complects blob construction, DOM mutation, and lifecycle cleanup in one handler.
issues.detail: EASY-NOT-SIMPLE. The familiar create-anchor-click-revoke dance is reachable but tangles 'what to download' (a value: filename + bytes) with 'how browsers trigger a save' (an effect). A small pure function that returns {fileName, blob} plus a separate triggerDownload effect would let either side be tested or reused. Not urgent, but the shape will repeat.

issues.description: The question that should have been asked: why is the server sending bytes the client already has a path to?
issues.detail: Hammock first. The compiled file lives on a path the extension already knows. The real question is whether the JupyterLab environment can serve that path directly (it can, via the contents API) instead of round-tripping the bytes through an RPC return value. If yes, the whole script_content field disappears and the download becomes a link.

issues.description: No encoding declared on the file read; the value's identity as text is assumed, not stated.
issues.detail: open(script_path) relies on the platform default encoding, then the string is wrapped in a Blob typed 'text/plain'. The script is Python source — its encoding should be named (utf-8) at the read site so the value's meaning does not depend on the locale of the machine that compiled it. Small fix, real correctness.

review.summary: The change works, and the user-visible feature is reasonable, but the shape complects three concerns that were previously separate: compiling a pipeline, knowing where its artifacts live, and serving the bytes of one of those artifacts. The script's contents are now snapshotted into the RPC response and carried as React state next to the path that already identifies the same file, with no time semantics tying the two together. The easy path — read the file on the server, stuff it in the response, blob-and-click on the client — is familiar, not simple; a download link against the existing path, or a dedicated read endpoint fired on click, would decompose cleanly. Recommend separating the compile result (identity) from the file contents (value-on-demand) before this pattern repeats for other artifacts.
